doc.title: Bill Crow interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, October 18, 1995

title: His mother's radio work and technology replacing live music
summary: Radio networks and sound movies wiped out his mother's paid singing and silent-film piano jobs.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Where I came from: parents, siblings and birth

blocks.x: Do you think that change is partly because of the entertainment that’s available every place you go?

Sure. I mean I saw it happen when I was a kid. My mother used to take the ferry to Seattle and ride the streetcar up over the hill down to where the radio station was, and on the local Seattle radio station she would sing songs or play the organ and make $5 for the program, something like that. But I mean that was a big income in those days, supplementing what my dad was making. Everybody was out of work and he was scuffling, and $5 really made the difference between whether we had meat on the table or not sometimes. And when the Seattle radio station joined the network and all the programs started coming out of Chicago, those jobs vanished. She continued to play on the radio but it was for free on church programs. So then her extra income came from playing at funerals and weddings and things like that. She had also participated in a previous automation where when she was a young girl she played the piano for the silent movies down in Arizona where she lived. And of course when sound came in, that wiped out all those little piano players and also all the pit orchestras in the big cities that used to play for the movies.
